title: Harrison's longitude clocks
hook: A self-taught carpenter built the clock that solved the longitude problem.
peek: In the 1700s, sailors could not reliably tell how far east or west they were. John Harrison, a carpenter from Yorkshire, spent decades building sea clocks accurate enough to answer the question, then had to fight for his reward.
lede: Sailors could long work out their latitude from the sun and stars, but longitude defeated them. The answer was time: compare local noon with the time at home, and the difference gives your position east or west. That needed a clock that kept time on a rolling ship. In 1714, Britain offered a prize of up to £20,000, and John Harrison, a Yorkshire carpenter, set out to win it.

bullets.text: Harrison's early clocks used gears made of wood, including lignum vitae, a dense tropical timber that releases its own oil. That meant they needed little lubrication, a common source of trouble in clocks of his day.
He built three large sea clocks over about 30 years, then changed course and made a pocket-watch-sized timekeeper now called H4. On a trial voyage to Jamaica in 1761 it kept time to within seconds.

The officials judging the prize were slow to accept a clock as the answer, and some favoured an astronomical method. With help from King George III, Harrison was finally awarded a large sum by Parliament in 1773.
The clocks fell into neglect until a naval officer, Rupert Gould, spent years restoring them in the 1920s and 1930s. They are now on display at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, and some still run.
Accurate longitude is what makes it possible to pin down a place like Point Nemo, the spot in the ocean farthest from any land, and to find your way back to it.
While Harrison worked on his sea clocks, Britain reformed its calendar and skipped 11 days in September 1752 to catch up with the rest of Europe.
